summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo ordered its land, lake and river borders closed for the elections on 30 December 2018. Congolese citizens returning from Burundi to vote were nevertheless allowed through Kavimvira, with transport arranged to polling stations. The announcement covered election day, but reports do not establish how long each crossing actually stopped operating.

verification.notes: Confirmed election-day order and the observed Kavimvira exception for returning voters; crossing-level duration remains unmeasured.

summary: Rwanda restricted some of its citizens’ travel to Uganda in 2019 amid allegations of insecurity and a diplomatic dispute, while foreigners and some travellers with permission continued to cross. Heavy trucks were separately diverted from Gatuna, officially for construction, and a June trial opening ended in renewed restrictions. Access widened in 2022: cargo and returnees were admitted in January, an outbound passenger bus crossed in March, and local shopping restrictions eased later that month. These changing permissions do not establish uninterrupted closure of all traffic from 2019 to 2022.

verification.notes: Separated the March outbound bus observation from two-way passenger reopening and retained selective permission, freight diversion and later shopping access.

summary: Reports described people being stopped at the Goma–Gisenyi crossings on 1 August 2019 after Ebola cases in Goma, although Congolese leaving Rwanda were reportedly exempt. A Rwandan minister acknowledged a temporary closure, while the health ministry said screening had only slowed movement. Travellers were reported crossing again that afternoon at Grande and Petite Barrière. The conflicting accounts leave the extent and precise length of the interruption uncertain.

verification.notes: Compared the disputed closure and screening accounts with same-day resumption at both Goma crossings; the description preserves that disagreement.

summary: Burundi refused entry to passengers arriving from Rwanda at Ruhwa in March 2020, citing COVID-19 concerns; Congolese transit travellers and schoolchildren were among those affected. Cargo resumed under separate arrangements in April, and groups of stranded Burundians later returned with permission. Selected passenger services through Ruhwa were operating by September 2022, before the formal October reopening. Access differed by crossing and traveller group, so no single date establishes a complete passenger reopening.

verification.notes: Checked Ruhwa passenger and school-access effects, separate cargo resumption, authorised returnees and the distinction between observed September services and formal October reopening.

summary: Rwanda restricted ordinary passenger movement across its land borders from 21 March 2020 to limit COVID-19 transmission. Goods, returning citizens and legal residents were exempt, with quarantine requirements for returnees, and later agreements admitted additional groups such as students and patients. National permission for land-border passenger travel resumed on 7 March 2022, although local documents and neighbouring countries’ rules continued to limit access at some crossings.

verification.notes: Verified the 21 March effective policy date, goods and citizen/resident exceptions, and March 2022 permission without implying every counterpart crossing opened.

summary: Uganda closed its land and water borders to most passenger entry and exit on 22 March 2020 as part of its COVID-19 response, while allowing cargo and its crews to cross. Permission for leisure and business travel returned on 1 October, but restrictions on people seeking asylum lasted longer. Exceptional refugee admissions took place in July 2020 and November 2021, and broader asylum access was reported in 2022; the evidence does not identify a single date when all such restrictions ended.

verification.notes: Changed October reopening to restored travel permission because that phase establishes policy; kept exceptional refugee movements separate from general asylum access.

summary: South Kivu authorities closed the Ruzizi I and II crossings between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda on 22 March 2020 to reduce the risk of importing COVID-19. A bilateral agreement on 11 November allowed specified groups, including students, teachers, doctors and patients, to cross with passports or laissez-passer. Local crossing tokens remained insufficient, so this was a limited relaxation rather than unrestricted passenger reopening.

verification.notes: Confirmed South Kivu’s March passenger measure and the November agreement for named traveller categories with specified documents, rather than unrestricted reopening.

summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo closed its borders to passengers under a COVID-19 emergency ordinance dated 24 March 2020, while exempting freight and applying health controls to cargo personnel. The president later scheduled border reopening for 15 August, and subsequent reporting confirmed that reopening. The transition from the July end of emergency measures to the August reopening is not fully documented, and national permission did not guarantee immediate access at every crossing.

verification.notes: Checked the March emergency ordinance, freight exemptions and August operational confirmation; the July announcement is not treated as an immediate border reopening.

summary: Burundi imposed renewed restrictions on land and water passenger travel from 11 January 2021 to curb COVID-19, while allowing goods to move. Repatriation convoys continued through Mugina and Gatumba under humanitarian arrangements. Ordinary passenger access resumed at Gatumba on 1 June and was authorised at Kobero–Kabanga and Mugina on 14 June, with testing and documentation conditions still in place.

verification.notes: Verified the January passenger restriction, continued goods traffic, authorised repatriations and different observed or announced June reopening dates.

summary: North Kivu’s military governor prohibited imports and exports through Bunagana on 20 June 2022 after M23 took control of the crossing, describing trade there as collaboration with the enemy. The order did not physically stop all commerce: journalists observed trade supervised by M23-appointed officials in April 2023. Plans to restore Congolese state services, and Uganda’s later reopening, do not establish when the Congolese prohibition was lifted.

verification.notes: Checked the North Kivu import/export prohibition, attributed collaboration allegation and later rebel-administered trade; none demonstrates repeal of the prohibition.

summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo ordered border restrictions for its 20 December 2023 elections. At Mpondwe–Kasindi, passengers and trucks were blocked from entering or leaving from 19–20 December and were still stopped on the afternoon of 21 December. Congolese returning to vote were separately admitted at Ruzizi. The first reopening at Mpondwe is unknown; later trade activity does not show that the election closure continued until then.

verification.notes: Verified the election order, Mpondwe’s observed closure bounds and Ruzizi voter exception; no unsupported reopening date is supplied.

summary: Burundi closed its land border with Rwanda on 11 January 2024 amid renewed diplomatic tensions and Burundian allegations that Rwanda supported armed groups. The decision disrupted trade and passenger travel, leaving people returning from markets stranded on both sides at Ruhwa. Travel advice continued to describe the ordinary land border as closed in October 2026, while air links remained available; exceptional permissions are not comprehensively documented.

verification.notes: Confirmed the January 2024 reclosure and attributed armed-group allegation; October 2026 status evidence still distinguishes closed land access from air links.

summary: Uganda suspended formal operations at Bunagana, Ishasha and Busanza in January 2025 as M23 controlled adjoining Congolese territory, while some informal movement continued. A separate March customs instruction redirected DRC-bound goods from six posts, including routes through Rwanda, citing revenue losses after Kinshasa lost control of Goma and Bukavu. July reopening permissions concerned the three suspended posts; they do not establish repeal of the separate routing instruction. August reporting still distinguished small local trucks from restricted heavy international freight.

verification.notes: Clarified that July reopening permissions concerned the January suspensions and do not prove repeal of the distinct March goods-routing instruction.

summary: Fighting during M23’s capture of Goma interrupted passenger and trading movement at the border with Rwanda in January 2025. Petite Barrière traffic stopped on 26 January, and the main crossing was reported closed the next day, apart from some UN evacuations. Grande Barrière admitted refugees into Rwanda on 28 January; ordinary travel and trade at Petite Barrière were observed by 4 February, although its first reopening date is uncertain.

verification.notes: Checked the separate Petite and main-crossing closures, evacuation and refuge exceptions, and February observation of ordinary Petite access without assigning a first reopening date.

summary: Burundian police blocked travellers heading towards Uvira on 10 December 2025 as M23 advanced, and the Gatumba–Kavimvira crossing was reported fully closed the following day. The restriction affected traders, patients and other travellers, although the South Kivu governor was allowed to cross in January. Ordinary movement resumed on 23 February 2026 within announced opening hours of 08:00–17:00. Later accounts disagree over the original closure date, so the contemporary December reports provide the clearest starting bounds.

verification.notes: Matched December 10 outward blockage and December 11 full closure to contemporary reports, and the February 23 actual reopening with hours and governor exception.

summary: Burundi’s interior minister reportedly announced on 1 October 2026 that people arriving from, or having travelled through, AFC-M23-controlled areas would be denied entry, including UN personnel. The report linked the decision to security concerns and support for the Congolese government. An effective date and implementation of this broad ban have not been established; earlier reports of refusals involving M23-issued documents concern a narrower rule.

verification.notes: Retained the reported announcement and unresolved implementation while removing the dataset-exclusion sentence from the public description.

summary: Burundian authorities restricted travel across the Rwanda border during a prolonged political dispute, linking reopening to diplomatic normalisation and demands for the return of alleged coup participants. In March 2022, Burundian traders were still being refused passage at Ruhwa. An August permission allowed a named transport company’s Congolese and Burundian clients through, and broader access without ministry permits was observed on 30 September, before official reopening confirmation in October. The original onset and uninterrupted extent of the restrictions remain uncertain.

verification.notes: Checked March refusals, the agency-specific August permission and September actual access before October confirmation; no uninterrupted political-closure span is inferred.

summary: Ethiopia and Eritrea reopened the Bure–Debay Sima and Zalambessa–Serha road crossings on 11 September 2018 after restrictions associated with their war and prolonged military standoff. Civilian reunions at the crossings demonstrated renewed passenger access, and the roads also served trade. Accounts describe roughly twenty years of closure beginning in 1998, but do not establish an exact starting day or exclude every intervening exception. Renewed restrictions later in 2018 and 2019 were separate episodes.

verification.notes: Verified both September 11 crossing names and civilian reunions; the twenty-year retrospective supports year-level onset only and excludes later reclosures.

summary: Sudan declared its border with South Sudan closed again on 29 March 2016, accusing its neighbour of supporting rebels; South Sudan denied the allegation. The restriction remained official policy in April, although people continued entering Sudan by paid transport and on foot. Later reports described functioning corridors, including Jebelein–Renk in 2021. These observations show that the frontier was not continuously sealed, but do not establish the first reopening of the 2016 restriction.

verification.notes: Confirmed March 29 declaration and April continued policy despite actual arrivals, with 2021 corridor operation not treated as the first reopening.

summary: Kenya formally closed its land border with Somalia in October 2011 amid security concerns involving al-Shabaab, affecting ordinary travel and commerce at named crossings. Enforcement was uneven, with officials later acknowledging that some posts were closed only on paper. A planned 2023 reopening was postponed, and 2026 permission for road exports of miraa did not amount to general passenger reopening. Travel advice in October 2026 continued to describe the land border as closed.

verification.notes: Updated the final status observation using the October 2026 status review; preserved uneven enforcement and distinction between miraa permission and general reopening.

summary: Sudan ordered its Eritrea crossings closed on the evening of 5 January 2018 under emergency measures aimed at illicit arms, drugs and trafficking. Contemporary reporting nevertheless described legal procedures for nationals entering or leaving through Laffa, without establishing who actually crossed. The restriction was still described in January 2019, when reopening was announced. Subsequent talks and a later Laffa opening do not establish the first resumption of ordinary traffic or a continuous closure through intervening years.

verification.notes: Checked January 5 evening onset and Laffa procedures; January 2019 announcement, later talks and 2023 ceremony do not time first ordinary passage.

summary: Eritrean controls restricted Ethiopian citizens and Ethiopian-registered vehicles entering through Rama and Zalambessa in late December 2018, shortly after the crossings had reopened. Reports disagree over which post introduced restrictions first, placing the changes on 26–27 December. Eritreans could reportedly return to Eritrea and Ethiopians could leave it. Business disruption at Zalambessa was still documented in May 2019; the precise reason and first subsequent reopening of these entry restrictions remain uncertain.

verification.notes: Compared the conflicting Rama/Zalambessa order with permitted return directions and May business disruption; the uncertainty and lack of an identified reopening remain explicit.

summary: Eritrean authorities restricted movement at the remaining road crossings with Ethiopia in April 2019. Non-Eritreans were being refused entry at Omhajer by 18 April, while Ethiopia continued admitting Eritrean nationals; Bure was reported closed on 22 April and remained so in reporting five days later. No crossing-specific official explanation or first reopening was established, and the Omhajer exception cannot automatically be applied to Bure.

verification.notes: Verified Omhajer non-Eritrean entry denial by April 18 and Bure April 22–27 reports; retained the crossing-specific direction and limited exception.

summary: Sudan’s military announced the closure of land borders during the takeover on 11 April 2019. Egyptian passengers and students stranded in Sudan were subsequently allowed to return through Arqin, where instructions took effect on the morning of 13 April and buses were reported arriving in Egypt. That facilitated return establishes access for this group at Arqin, rather than a reopening date for all Sudanese land crossings.

verification.notes: Confirmed military announcement, continuing closure on April 12 and observed Egyptian return buses at Arqin April 13; no nationwide reopening is inferred.

summary: South Sudan restricted ordinary passenger travel across its borders on 23–24 March 2020 to limit COVID-19 transmission, while exempting food, fuel, medical supplies and emergency relief. The national travel ban was lifted on 11 May, but land-passenger restrictions continued at some crossings, including Nimule. Passenger access on the Uganda route was reported restored in the first half of October. The national policy change and the later resumption of that route therefore describe different stages.

verification.notes: Expressed the Uganda-route resumption as the first half of October to match October 1–15 bounds and retained separate national policy and operational stages.

summary: The Diffra crossing in the Abyei area stopped handling ordinary incoming movements from South Sudan during Sudan’s COVID-19 restrictions in March 2020. IOM reported that the point reopened in July and registered incoming South Sudanese travellers. The evidence establishes the months of closure and reopening, rather than exact days, and does not show that all other Sudanese border crossings or categories of traveller followed the same timetable.

verification.notes: Checked IOM’s March-to-July Diffra account and registered incoming South Sudanese; month bounds and the limited route and cohort are retained.

summary: Ethiopia announced an immediate restriction on land-border passenger movement on 23 March 2020 to curb COVID-19, while allowing essential goods and later expressly confirming freight exemptions in both directions. Services with Djibouti resumed during July or by 7 August, according to later reports. That resumption concerns the Djibouti route; it does not establish when passenger travel resumed at Ethiopia’s other borders or the exact first crossing after reopening.

verification.notes: Confirmed March order and April freight exemptions, and the July-to-August 7 Djibouti resumption bound without transferring it to other neighbours.

summary: COVID-19 restrictions closed the Dollow bridge between Somalia and Ethiopia in March 2020, preventing workers from reaching jobs, disrupting small traders and stopping refugees from making usual visits. Interviews in mid-April described the continuing interruption to ordinary movement and goods carried across the bridge. Some produce still arrived by informal river boats. Gedo officials also reported other crossings closed, but the first reopening of the Dollow bridge has not been established.

verification.notes: Verified bridge-specific March disruption and April interviews, both worker/refugee movement and carried goods, with informal river traffic kept distinct.

summary: Kenya barred passenger movement in both directions across its Tanzania and Somalia borders from the night of 16–17 May 2020 to reduce COVID-19 transmission. Cargo vehicles remained permitted subject to driver testing, and locally identified farmers later received permission to reach plots across the Tanzania border. The passenger prohibition was still reported in June. Passenger services through Namanga were operating by October 2021, but that does not establish their first reopening or the outcome at Somalia crossings.

verification.notes: Checked the overnight effective date, two-direction passenger scope, cargo testing and farmer exception; Namanga’s later service cannot date Somalia reopening.

summary: Djibouti ordered a new fifteen-day restriction on land-border passenger travel from 20 October 2020 in response to COVID-19, exempting goods and returning Djiboutian nationals. Reporting described implementation from 21 October, while some migrant movement continued. Travel advice in December described the borders as open subject to testing. The planned fifteen-day limit does not establish the exact day ordinary passenger crossings resumed.

verification.notes: Verified decree versus implementation dates, IOM’s returning-national exception and December open-status advice; the fifteen-day schedule is not presented as observed reopening.

summary: Kassala’s governor ordered the Sudanese state’s border with Ethiopia closed on 5 November 2020 as fighting began in Tigray, saying armed entrants would not be admitted. By 11 November, UNHCR and local authorities were receiving, screening and registering Ethiopian refugees at Hamdayet. Those admissions show that the order did not prevent all entry, but do not establish when ordinary travel or trade resumed.

verification.notes: Confirmed the Kassala governor’s November 5 order and the November 11 Hamdayet refugee admissions; ordinary trade or travel reopening remains unestablished.

summary: Sudanese authorities closed Gallabat on 3 April 2021 after an attack on customs officers near the Ethiopian border, with reopening linked to action against those responsible. Permission to reopen followed on 4 April, and more than fifteen Sudanese trucks carrying cooking gas into Ethiopia were reported crossing on 5 April. The agreement also addressed workers and other goods, but their first resumed movements were not separately observed.

verification.notes: Checked April 3 closure after the earlier attack, April 4 permission and April 5 gas-truck passage towards Ethiopia, without extending that observation to all categories.

summary: Sudan restricted travel and commerce through Gallabat–Metema from 24 July 2021 after a Sudanese officer disappeared and was subsequently reported killed. Authorities sought action against those responsible, while gas trucks received exemptions and some paid passage was alleged. Reports describe an intervening reopening and renewed restrictions in January 2022 before movement resumed on 2 March. The episode therefore involved changing access rather than one uninterrupted closure of all traffic.

verification.notes: Compared July onset, contested January access and gas exceptions with March 2 movement; the intermittent interpretation avoids unsupported continuous closure.

summary: Ordinary passenger movement and non-fuel trade through Gallabat–Metema were restricted again in the first half of January 2022. Sudanese authorities cited security concerns and demands for prosecution of the kidnappers of a Sudanese officer. Gas or fuel trucks received separate humanitarian permissions, and some paid passage was alleged. Ordinary movement resumed on 2 March, but the exact January onset is uncertain and this reclosure overlaps the longer episode beginning in July 2021.

verification.notes: Verified January 1–15 onset bounds, distinct fuel permissions and March 2 ordinary resumption; overlap with the July episode is disclosed.

summary: Sudan closed Gallabat–Metema on 27 June 2022 following the disputed deaths of Sudanese soldiers, interrupting passenger and commercial movement along the Ethiopian frontier. The competing accounts of the killings were not resolved. Sudan authorised reopening on 17 July after confidence-building measures; dry-port services reportedly resumed on 21 July, and regular flows were reported after that date. Permission to reopen and the subsequent return of traffic are therefore distinct dates.

verification.notes: Distinguished July 21 dry-port service from IOM’s flows after that date and preserved July 17 as the permission date.

summary: Fighting involving Fano forces interrupted civilian travel and commerce at Gallabat–Metema on 1–2 September 2024. Negotiated passages allowed some disarmed Ethiopian security personnel and stranded Sudanese to cross. Cross-border movement resumed around 21–22 October, but reports later described missing immigration, visa and customs services. Subsequent restrictions on regular travellers coexisted with local movement and specially cleared returns, so the September closure cannot be extended as an uninterrupted ban on everyone.

verification.notes: Checked conflicting September and October dates, negotiated exceptions and later missing services; subsequent regular-traveller restrictions remain distinct from this closure.

summary: Djibouti restricted land-border passenger travel under COVID-19 decrees beginning in March 2020, while exempting goods. Successive orders maintained restrictions before land and sea reopening was authorised for 17 July, subject to testing. Passenger trains between Djibouti and Ethiopia followed a separate timetable: suspension was announced from 20 March, and the operator reported their return on 27 January 2021. These dates describe different modes and do not establish identical access at every crossing.

verification.notes: Verified separate decree windows, July land/sea permission and March-to-January train suspension; the description does not claim identical operational dates across modes.

summary: Eritrea applied COVID-19 restrictions to overland passenger travel in 2020, adding to pre-existing restrictions at some borders. Government statements linked the measures to the pandemic but also acknowledged people continuing to arrive and enter quarantine. Later assessments still described land borders as closed to ordinary travel while permitting screened cargo. The exact land-specific starting date, extent of enforcement and distinction from older bilateral closures remain uncertain.

verification.notes: Confirmed the COVID-specific attribution alongside acknowledged arrivals and cargo screening; no precise land onset or separation from every older restriction is asserted.

summary: Togo ordered a temporary land-border closure around its municipal elections on 30 June 2019. Official reporting described closure from Saturday evening to Sunday evening, while another account gave midnight Sunday to midnight Monday. These accounts describe a short election-related restriction, but disagree over its hours; they do not establish a two-day closure or the actual time traffic resumed.

verification.notes: Compared official evening-to-evening wording and the alternative midnight schedule; neither supports two days or observed resumed traffic.

summary: Togo ordered its land borders closed on 17 July 2025 for municipal election security, with the announced restriction running from 00:00 to 23:59. Air and sea borders were to remain open. The available notice does not specify separate passenger, freight or nationality exceptions, and does not establish the actual time operations stopped and resumed at individual land crossings.

verification.notes: Checked the exact July 17 ordered window and open air/sea borders; unspecified exceptions and unobserved implementation remain qualified.

summary: Benin initially announced that its land borders would close from midnight on 11 January 2026 until 06:00 on 12 January for legislative and municipal election security. Before the measure took effect, the government reversed the decision and said the borders would remain open on election day. The planned thirty-hour restriction was therefore cancelled, and an implemented election closure has not been established.

verification.notes: Removed dataset-reference language while preserving the initial thirty-hour proposal and its January 10 cancellation before implementation.

summary: Togo ordered all land borders closed for its legislative elections from midnight on 20 December 2018 until midnight the following day. The government presented the measure as supporting peaceful and secure polling. Reports do not specify separate freight or directional exceptions, nor confirm the actual first passage after the order ended. The announced window was twenty-four hours, rather than a restriction lasting more than one day.

verification.notes: Verified the December 20–21 midnight schedule, government election-security reason and lack of observed reopening; the twenty-four-hour duration remains explicitly an order.

summary: Nigeria restored customs clearance for Cotonou-origin trucks travelling through Tsamiya and Kamba towards Niger on 9 February 2026, after officials described months of restrictions and stranded freight. Nigerian officials cited security and the regulation of lawful trade, with reports also referring to smuggling and unpaid transit taxes. Accounts differ over earlier responsibility for the blockage. The evidence concerns this transit-freight route and does not establish a continuous closure from 2019 or a corresponding passenger ban.

verification.notes: Confirmed February 9 truck clearance and Nigerian responsibility for reopening, while preserving conflicting earlier attribution and unknown onset.

summary: Nigeria ordered its land borders closed from noon on 15 February 2019 for elections scheduled the following day. When polling was postponed, the government reversed the closure on 16 February rather than waiting until its planned expiry on 17 February. People and vehicles were reported crossing at Seme early that Saturday, with normal customs and immigration checks. The precise stopping and restarting times at every border post are not established.

verification.notes: Checked the cancelled February 15–17 schedule against actual February 16 Seme passage after election postponement; no national synchronized reopening is claimed.

summary: Nigeria ordered its land borders closed for the rescheduled presidential election from noon on 22 February 2019 until noon on 24 February. The immigration notice described a nationwide restriction on movement during polling, without specifying individual crossing rules or freight exemptions. One report gave a different ending hour, and actual reopening was not independently timed. The principal notice records a forty-eight-hour planned closure, not a measured forty-eight-hour stoppage at every post.

verification.notes: Verified the signed noon-to-noon rescheduled-election notice and conflicting midnight report, with the unrelated February 16 opening excluded.

summary: Nigeria ordered its external land borders closed from noon on 8 March 2019 until noon on 10 March for governorship and state elections. The immigration announcement describes a nationwide election measure without detailing separate freight or traveller exceptions. A conflicting report gave a midnight timetable, and the actual first reopening was not established. The noon-to-noon schedule is therefore recorded as a planned restriction rather than a measured stoppage at every crossing.

verification.notes: Compared the immigration-attributed March 8–10 noon schedule with the midnight discrepancy; neither supplies actual first reopening.

summary: Nigeria began a border-enforcement operation on 20 August 2019 aimed at smuggling, restricting otherwise admissible goods through crossings including Seme–Kraké. Selected companies and some consignments received permissions, while passenger rules later overlapped COVID-19 controls. The government authorised reopening on 16 December 2020 but retained rice and poultry import bans. Backlogged goods were not all released immediately, so that policy decision does not establish a single date when every cargo movement resumed.

verification.notes: Checked August enforcement onset, December permission and retained product bans; release authorisations are not confused with actual clearance of every consignment.

summary: Togo restricted ordinary passenger travel across its land borders from the night of 20–21 March 2020 to curb COVID-19, while allowing commercial goods to move. Some schoolchildren and vaccinated border residents were still able to cross at Aflao–Lomé before the general reopening. The government authorised ordinary land-border travel again from 17 May 2022, subject to vaccination conditions. The policy period therefore included exceptions rather than complete denial of all passenger movement.

verification.notes: Verified the overnight March order, goods exception, observed students/residents and May 17 vaccination-conditioned policy reopening.

summary: Senegal and the Gambia announced a twenty-one-day border restriction on 23–24 March 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission, exempting security personnel, foodstuffs and medical services. Senegal continued requiring special clearance and a negative test for intending travellers in October, even after the Gambia lifted its own restrictions. Later reopening reports do not establish the first ordinary crossing date. This chronology concerns Senegal’s side of the Gambia frontier, rather than all Senegalese borders.

verification.notes: Confirmed Gambia-frontier-specific bilateral order, October Senegal clearance requirements and unreliable later endpoint claims; scope is not expanded nationwide.

summary: Ghana restricted ordinary passenger entry across its land borders from 22 March 2020 as part of its COVID-19 response, while exempting goods, supplies and cargo. The government maintained the land-travel restriction after some other travel resumed, then lifted it from 28 March 2022 with vaccination and testing conditions. Authorised exceptions and neighbouring countries’ rules meant that neither the closure nor reopening produced identical access for every traveller at every crossing.

verification.notes: Checked March 22 entry restriction and March 28 lifting against presidential texts, retaining cargo, authorised travellers and counterpart controls.

summary: Côte d’Ivoire restricted passenger movement across its borders from 22 March 2020 to curb COVID-19, while allowing goods subject to health checks and special humanitarian or security corridors. Land-border reopening was ordered in February 2023, and two-way passenger traffic at Noé–Elubo was observed on 16 February. Residents also described some earlier paid family passage. The observed reopening concerns that crossing and does not establish identical implementation at every frontier post.

verification.notes: Verified March passenger scope and health-controlled goods, followed by observed February 16 two-way Noé–Elubo traffic and attributed earlier family passage.

summary: The Gambia and Senegal announced an initial twenty-one-day land-border restriction in March 2020 to limit COVID-19, exempting food, medical services and security personnel. A later Gambian closure policy, dated from 19 May, was lifted on 16 October when the government authorised land and sea reopening. Senegal still required special clearance and a negative test for entry several days later. Gambian reopening therefore did not immediately mean unrestricted passage in both directions.

verification.notes: Compared the separate March ordered window and May-to-October policy with October 16 lifting, preserving Senegal’s continuing entry requirements.

summary: Liberia restricted passenger access towards Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire from 30 March 2020 during the COVID-19 response, disrupting travel and markets at Ganta. Goods could still move through humanitarian permissions, transfers at the frontier or replacement by local drivers. An official at Ganta reported restored traveller access under health controls by March 2021, while another account suggests earlier reopening on the Guinea route. The conflicting reports do not establish one exact reopening date or continuous closure at every post.

verification.notes: Checked the Guinea/Côte d’Ivoire onset, commercial-goods arrangements and Ganta official access report; conflicting earlier opening accounts remain unresolved.

summary: Mali’s military authorities ordered the country’s borders closed from 19 August 2020 after taking power in a coup. They authorised air and land borders to reopen from midnight on 21 August. These are the dates of the Malian government’s own order; the separate ECOWAS sanctions imposed by neighbouring states continued under a different timetable. The available announcement does not establish the first resumed passage at each crossing.

verification.notes: Verified the Malian military’s August 19 order and August 21 permission independently of ECOWAS member restrictions.

summary: ECOWAS imposed border and commercial sanctions on Mali on 18 August 2020 after the military coup, seeking restoration of constitutional government. Summit statements subsequently exempted essential food, medicines, fuel and electricity. The sanctions were lifted through a decision adopted on 5 October and announced the following day. These regional policy dates do not establish uniform enforcement at every border, and Mali’s earlier decision to reopen its own crossings did not end its neighbours’ restrictions.

verification.notes: Confirmed regional sanctions and humanitarian exceptions, and the October 5 adoption versus October 6 announcement distinction.

summary: Guinea restricted its land frontier with Senegal in September 2020 ahead of Guinea’s presidential election, with an unnamed official citing security reasons. The restriction remained in place despite a June 2021 agreement intended to restore access, with reports in July saying implementation was still pending. Guinea’s military authorities later authorised reopening from 29 September 2021. The original September starting day and the conditions experienced by every traveller are not established, so the policy dates should not be read as an exact account of all crossing activity.

verification.notes: Checked the September month bounds without borrowing Guinea-Bissau’s exact day, the unimplemented June agreement and September 2021 permission.

summary: Guinea closed its side of the Guinea-Bissau border from 27 September 2020 during the pre-election period, restricting people and goods; an unnamed official attributed the measure to security concerns. Reopening was announced for late September 2021, with accounts differing between 27 and 28 September. A reporter observed a dried-fish truck entering Guinea at Saare Bhoydho–Kandikka on 28 September after checks; vaccination was also required. That observation confirms restored access at one crossing without establishing identical conditions at every post.

verification.notes: Checked September 27 onset, conflicting reopening notices and actual September 28 fish-truck entry with vaccination controls at the named crossing.

summary: Guinea’s military authorities closed borders after the coup on 5 September 2021, adding new restrictions on several frontiers to older closures facing Senegal and Guinea-Bissau. At Pamelap on the Sierra Leone border, reopening was authorised on 16 September and reported in operation from 06:00 the next day. An earlier national permission for commercial and humanitarian movement did not establish that ordinary local access had resumed. The confirmed reopening here concerns Pamelap specifically.

verification.notes: Verified the new coup-related scope and Pamelap’s September 17 implementation; earlier general commercial permission does not replace that local observation.

summary: ECOWAS ordered border sanctions against Mali on 9 January 2022 in response to the proposed delay in elections, exempting food, medicines, petroleum products and electricity. Implementation varied: Guinea refused to close its border, clinker was later observed crossing at Tengrela, and livestock movements received separate authorisations. ECOWAS lifted the sanctions on 3 July. The regional policy therefore restricted trade and travel without producing a uniform blockade of every Malian frontier.

verification.notes: Made observed clinker traffic and merely authorised livestock movements explicitly different, while retaining Guinea’s refusal and the regional lifting date.

summary: Burkina Faso’s military authorities ordered land borders closed on 24 January 2022 after the coup. The following day they exempted humanitarian vehicles, essential goods and defence or security supplies, while air travel followed separate reopening arrangements. The land-border order was lifted on 2 February. These official dates describe a temporary policy with exceptions; the first actual resumption of each ordinary crossing is not separately documented.

verification.notes: Confirmed January 24 national order, January 25 specified land exceptions and February 2 policy lifting, with air reopening kept separate.

summary: Burkina Faso’s military authorities announced another border closure on the night of 30 September–1 October 2022 following a coup. A subsequent communiqué exempted humanitarian vehicles, freight and vehicles carrying defence or security supplies. The national closure order was lifted on 4 October. The sources leave the precise midnight starting convention uncertain and do not independently time the first resumed passage at each land crossing.

verification.notes: Checked the midnight onset ambiguity and humanitarian, freight and defence exceptions against the October 4 lifting notice.

summary: Nigeria ordered all land borders closed to the movement of people from midnight on 25 February 2023 until midnight the following day for the presidential election. The interior minister said the measure would prevent external disruption and protect life and property. The circular did not separately detail cargo treatment or exceptions. Its twenty-four-hour schedule does not establish the exact period for which every crossing stopped operating.

verification.notes: Verified the February 25–26 person-movement circular, attributed election-security purpose and absence of cargo or actual gate-timing evidence.

summary: Nigeria ordered its external land borders closed from midnight on 18 March 2023 until midnight on 19 March for state elections. The directive covered the country’s land frontiers, while separate state-level movement controls applied inside Nigeria. Reports do not establish detailed border exceptions or the actual time traffic resumed. The announced restriction lasted twenty-four hours and should not be read as evidence of a longer operational shutdown.

verification.notes: Confirmed March 18–19 external-land-border schedule and kept domestic state controls distinct; the prospective notice does not establish longer enforcement.

summary: Niger’s military authorities closed the country’s borders after taking power on 26 July 2023. They authorised reopening towards Algeria, Burkina Faso, Libya, Mali and Chad from 1 August, while Nigeria and Benin were outside that partial reversal. The decree covered land and air borders, but reports did not establish the first resumed traffic at each gate. Its timetable therefore records Niger’s own policy, rather than simultaneous restoration of every regional route.

verification.notes: Checked July 26 onset and the numeric August 1 decree date despite the source weekday error, with only the five named neighbours covered by the reversal.

summary: Niger kept the official Gaya–Malanville road crossing with Benin closed after ECOWAS lifted sanctions in February 2024, despite Benin reopening its side. Niger alleged that French bases in Benin posed a security threat and cited this as its reason for refusing to reopen. Passengers and goods continued using informal river routes. Later reports of road reopening conflicted, while official restrictions were still described in October 2026, leaving the timing and extent of any intervening access uncertain.

verification.notes: Preserved the October 2026 continuing formal restriction, conflicting intermediate reopening accounts and informal river traffic, while removing review-oriented wording from the attributed allegation.

summary: ECOWAS imposed land-border and commercial sanctions on Niger on 30 July 2023, demanding President Mohamed Bazoum’s release and restoration after the coup. Implementation varied between neighbouring states, and humanitarian agencies reported that aid on the Benin route remained blocked despite disputed claims about exemptions; alternative routes continued operating. ECOWAS lifted the sanctions on 24 February 2024. That regional decision did not mean every border reopened at once.

verification.notes: Verified July 30 and February 24 regional decisions, attributed humanitarian-access dispute and alternative routes without claiming universal member compliance.

summary: Nigeria restricted its Illela crossing with Niger during the ECOWAS sanctions imposed after Niger’s July 2023 coup, while allowing some returning Nigerians to enter. Nigerian customs reopened its side on 14 March 2024, but Niger-side restrictions continued at Birni N’Konni. Two-way traffic was reported returning on 22 March. Informal movement had continued during the restriction, and the staggered reopening at this route does not establish the same timetable for every Nigeria–Niger crossing.

verification.notes: Compared Illela onset bounds and returnee exception with March 14 Nigerian permission and March 22 bilateral traffic, retaining informal passage and gate-specific scope.

summary: Ghana ordered all land borders closed with immediate effect on 6 December 2024 until 18:00 on 8 December, saying the measure would protect the integrity of the 7 December general election. The order addressed travellers entering and leaving Ghana, while Kotoka airport remained open. It did not specify a starting hour or separate cargo exemptions, and actual reopening at individual gates was not observed in the available evidence.

verification.notes: Checked the signed December 6 immediate order and December 8 18:00 expiry; no start clock, cargo exception or observed gate reopening is invented.

summary: Civilian entry and exit at the Yenga–Koindu–Nongoa crossing on the Makona River were restricted on 27–28 April 2025 amid the territorial dispute between Guinea and Sierra Leone. Residents and traders lost access to a local route for people and agricultural goods, although clandestine passage was reported. A ministry notice later dated formal reopening to 24 June 2026, and boats carrying people and goods were observed in August. The evidence concerns this local crossing, not the entire bilateral frontier.

verification.notes: Verified April 27–28 local river-crossing bounds, ministry-attributed June reopening and August observed boats, with clandestine trade distinct from authorised exceptions.

summary: Guinea ordered land and maritime borders closed around the presidential election on 28 December 2025 as part of measures to protect voters, candidates, electoral staff and materials. The land-border order was interpreted as covering polling day through the following midnight. Air-border hours and domestic vehicle restrictions followed separate provisions. The available announcement does not establish actual enforcement at each crossing or the first resumed movement.

verification.notes: Compared the signed order’s land/maritime wording with separate air and domestic provisions; retained the polling-day interpretation and unobserved actual reopening.

summary: Guinea restricted its frontier with Sierra Leone in September 2020 under a national security measure. A bilateral agreement later authorised reopening from 08:00 on 18 February 2021, and a correspondent observed the crossing opening around that time. The national account dates the restriction to September, while the local report places closure later in the year. The evidence therefore supports reopening but leaves the exact starting date of local enforcement uncertain.

verification.notes: Compared national September onset with the correspondent’s later local recollection and confirmed actual February 18 opening near the agreed 08:00 time.

summary: Guinea-Bissau restricted part of its Senegal frontier on 17–19 June 2024 after communal clashes at Médina Gounass. The president said the aim was to stop reinforcements leaving Guinea-Bissau to join the violence in Senegal. The affected posts, treatment of goods and exceptions were not specified. Reports confirm the announced restriction but do not establish a reopening date or show that the entire bilateral border was closed.

verification.notes: Verified bounded June announcement, partial frontier and outward reinforcement-prevention purpose; no full-border scope, exact duration or later continuation is inferred.

summary: Reuters reported that the Gambia’s land borders were closed during the presidential election on 1 December 2016, citing a Western diplomatic source rather than direct observation at the crossings. The affected posts and exceptions were not established. A journalist subsequently described crossing from Senegal into the Gambia near Karang in January 2017, but that later access does not reveal when the election restriction ended or whether it persisted continuously.

verification.notes: Checked Reuters’ explicitly unverified diplomatic-source report and the later Karang entry; January access is not converted into an election-closure endpoint.

summary: Benin restricted land entry and exit to indispensable journeys from 17 March 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission, with crossings coordinated with neighbouring authorities. Goods, including relief supplies, continued to move while passenger restrictions remained in place in April. By March 2022, government rules expressly allowed entry by land subject to testing, although no exact repeal or first reopening was established. Removal of testing documents in June was a later change, not the first evidence of ordinary access.

verification.notes: Confirmed March essential-only policy and April goods flows, then March 2022 ordinary-entry permission before the separate June testing removal.

summary: Chad closed its frontier with Libya on 3 March 2019 after rebel incursions, with the government citing armed groups and trafficking. Subsequent assessments described interrupted supplies to Tibesti and continuing limits on income and market access in April. These reports support a sustained restriction, but do not identify the precise reopening date or every exception. Later permissions for selected northern routes cannot automatically be treated as the end of this closure.

verification.notes: Checked March 3 immediate closure, official armed-group/trafficking explanation and later Tibesti supply impacts; selective August routes do not fix an endpoint.

summary: Chad announced tighter controls on its Libya, Sudan and Central African Republic frontiers in August 2019, directing entry and exit through selected corridors for security reasons. Named routes remained available, including Adré and Tiné towards Sudan and Sido and Goré towards the Central African Republic. Reports differed over the list of northern passages, while later fieldwork described continued supply restrictions. The measure therefore channelled movement through specified routes rather than sealing all three borders.

verification.notes: Compared inconsistent corridor counts and lists with the minister’s selective-routing qualification; open Sudan/CAR passages and unknown final duration are retained.

summary: Burkina Faso restricted land and rail passenger travel from the night of 21–22 March 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission, while exempting freight. A decree authorised both modes to reopen from 1 December 2021. Reporters subsequently saw access restored near Yendéré and Léraba, but buses still faced limits because Côte d’Ivoire’s side remained formally closed. Health requirements and neighbouring rules therefore continued to shape travel after Burkina Faso lifted its own restriction.

verification.notes: Verified overnight March land/rail restriction, freight exception and December policy reopening, alongside local observations of continued Ivorian-side bus limits.

summary: Benin ordered its adjacent land borders closed from midnight on 17 May 2020 until 06:00 on 18 May for municipal elections. The interior minister described the measure as supporting orderly and peaceful voting. The notice did not detail crossing-specific traffic rules or exceptions, and the first actual reopening was not observed. The thirty-hour planned window overlapped separate COVID-19 restrictions, which cannot be treated as additional days of the same election closure.

verification.notes: Confirmed May 17 00:00–May 18 06:00 election schedule and ministerial purpose; no enforcement duration is borrowed from the overlapping pandemic rules.

summary: Niger ordered temporary restrictions at its land and river borders for the presidential runoff on 21 February 2021, while exempting land freight. Reports described a twenty-four-hour election-day measure but used differing midnight conventions, leaving the precise start and ending dates within overnight bounds. The announcement does not establish actual stopping or reopening times at individual crossings, and its separate air-travel provisions do not define this land-border episode.

verification.notes: Checked land/river scope and freight exception against differing midnight wording; the twenty-four-hour announcement remains separate from actual gate operations.

summary: Benin ordered its land borders closed on 8 January 2023 for legislative elections, with reopening scheduled for 06:00 on 9 January. The government presented the measure as supporting peaceful and orderly polling. The notice did not give an exact starting hour or detailed traffic exceptions, and no first resumed passage was documented, leaving the actual duration at individual crossings uncertain.

verification.notes: Removed the extraneous market-timetable explanation while retaining the missing border start hour and unobserved operational reopening.

summary: Liberia ordered authorised and unauthorised land frontiers with Guinea, Sierra Leone and Côte d’Ivoire closed ahead of the 10 October 2023 elections. Officials described election safety and prevention of foreign interference as the purposes, explicitly prohibiting entry. Reports placed closure from the evening of 9 October until the morning or noon of 11 October. The ending hour differed between accounts, and neither establishes actual reopening or the full treatment of outbound travellers.

verification.notes: Compared the 08:00 and noon ending reports with the October 9 evening start, explicit entry prohibition and separately attributed election-security reasons.

summary: Liberia’s Joint Security ordered the land borders with Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire and Sierra Leone closed from 12 November 2023 to protect the frontier during the presidential runoff on 14 November. The announcement said the restriction would last until the electoral process ended, without specifying traffic exceptions or individual posts. That wording does not establish reopening on polling day, and the first actual return of cross-border movement remains unknown.

verification.notes: Verified November 12 order and the open-ended electoral-process wording; polling day is not mistaken for an observed reopening.

summary: Guinea-Bissau’s military authorities announced a national border closure on 26 November 2025 during a coup and electoral dispute, citing alleged destabilisation. The next day, the military said all borders were open again. These statements establish a formal reversal of the land-border order, but do not detail passenger or freight exceptions or the times when individual crossings actually stopped and resumed operating.

verification.notes: Checked November 26 military declaration and November 27 formal reversal, preserving the attributed destabilisation allegation and lack of gate observations.

summary: The Nimule–Elegu crossing between South Sudan and Uganda closed after police officers were killed on the afternoon of 12 May 2022. Police described restrictions on movement, including outward travel, amid armed attacks and instability in the town. A Friday-morning interview on 13 May reported traffic flowing normally again. The interruption affected travellers and trade, but exact hours and individual exceptions were not established; the reported afternoon-to-morning interval was less than a day.

verification.notes: Matched Thursday-afternoon closure and Friday-morning normal traffic to the two reports; retained both-direction effects and less-than-one-day qualification.

summary: Protests after a chief’s killing interrupted border services and truck processing at Nimule–Elegu on 11 July 2022. By the following day, buses were reported travelling from Uganda into South Sudan, although some drivers continued waiting in queues. Uganda’s military said its side remained operational, so the episode does not establish identical closure orders on both sides. Later reports of normal traffic confirm access but are not the first reopening.

verification.notes: Verified July 11 interruption and July 12 northbound bus passage; truck queues and Uganda’s statement preclude an identical bilateral closure interpretation.

summary: Truck drivers halted Uganda-bound cargo at Malaba in early January 2022 in protest at paid repeat COVID-19 tests and shorter certificate validity. The stoppage affected fuel and other freight, while reverse-direction trucks and traffic at Busia were reported moving in the early stages. Reports placed a settlement around 11 January, but some operators still awaited an official circular. That reported strike-ending agreement does not establish when the first trucks crossed or queues cleared.

verification.notes: Checked January 1–3 onset bounds, Uganda-bound freight scope and conflicting settlement/circular accounts; strike agreement is not treated as first resumed passage.

summary: Guinea-Bissau restricted ordinary land-border passenger travel from 18 March 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission, while exempting medical evacuations, medicines and essential food imports. Fish vendors were nevertheless reported turned back at Mpack, showing uneven treatment of small traders. The land restrictions were renewed in April, and later advice described borders open under health conditions by October. Earlier permission for international travel does not establish an exact first reopening at the land crossings.

verification.notes: Confirmed March 18 effective order, medical/essential-import exceptions and April renewal, then October land-open advice without transferring earlier general travel permission.

summary: Sierra Leone restricted land-border passenger movement with Guinea and Liberia on the night of 27–28 March 2020 to prevent imported COVID-19 cases. Essential commodities were exempt, and a temporary return window allowed some people stranded across the boundary to come home. Both land frontiers were still described as closed in early April, while later reporting placed land reopening in February 2021. The exact restoration of each route, particularly the Liberia frontier, is not established.

verification.notes: Verified overnight March start, essential goods and temporary return window, April continuation and February 2021 broad land reopening without a precise Liberia endpoint.

summary: Mauritania tightened entry for Malians during border tensions in April 2024, with buses and trucks affected at Koki Zamal. Reports described violent incidents in the border area and increasing refusals, but no published order established a precise common starting day or formal explanation. Malian residents and people with written authorisation were reportedly eligible, although some permit holders were also refused. The evidence concerns selective entry into Mauritania, not a complete two-way border closure.

verification.notes: Compared April Koki Zamal refusals and EFE’s selective eligibility with continued refusals of some permit holders; no formal rationale or full two-way closure is invented.

summary: Tanzanian authorities restricted Kenyan truck drivers entering at Horohoro in May 2020 during a dispute over COVID-19 testing, while allowing some third-country transit and goods transfers. A renewed dispute affected Kenyan trucks at Namanga in June. By 18 June, officials had announced reciprocal permission for crews to proceed without waiting for test results, although the first resumed Tanzania-bound passage was not timed. The May and June restrictions were separate episodes rather than a demonstrated continuous blockade.

verification.notes: Checked Horohoro’s May driver directive and exceptions separately from June Namanga dispute; June reciprocal permission does not time Tanzania-bound operational return.

summary: Niger restricted land-border passenger travel from the night of 19–20 March 2020 to combat COVID-19, initially announcing a renewable two-week measure and exempting goods transport. The government authorised land reopening on 17 June 2021. Interviews shortly afterwards described services returning gradually, with different experiences among transport operators. The permission date therefore marks a national policy change, rather than simultaneous restoration of every route or uniform enforcement throughout the preceding period.

verification.notes: Verified effective overnight March schedule rather than announcement date, freight exception and June 17 permission followed by gradual operator-reported resumption.

summary: Mali restricted ordinary passenger entry and exit through its land borders from 26 March 2020 as part of its COVID-19 measures, while allowing freight and essential supplies. A later decree authorised land-border reopening from midnight on 31 July. Air travel resumed under a separate timetable. The land-policy dates do not establish when the first passenger crossed at every post or imply that goods movement had stopped throughout the same period.

verification.notes: Confirmed March 26 effective land order and July 31 decree permission, with freight and the separate aviation date kept distinct.

summary: Togo ordered its land borders closed for legislative and regional elections on 29 April 2024, with a scheduled window from 00:00 to 23:59. Airports and the seaport remained open. Normal entries, exits and commercial activity were reported returning early on 30 April at Aflao and Hilacondji. Those observations confirm reopening at the two named posts, but do not establish identical hours at every crossing or an interruption lasting more than twenty-four hours.

verification.notes: Matched the April 29 scheduled window with early April 30 actual Aflao/Hilacondji traffic; neither nationwide identical hours nor strictly longer duration is inferred.

summary: Somaliland authorities ordered regional land travel restricted from 18:00 on 26 March 2020 for three weeks to prevent COVID-19 transmission, exempting essential food, fuel, water and medical supplies. The order covered routes towards Ethiopia and Djibouti and the de facto boundary with Somalia. A later announcement lifted regional land and sea restrictions from 30 June while retaining testing or quarantine. These notices do not establish the complete enforcement history at every crossing.

verification.notes: Checked the operative March 26 18:00 directive over introductory shorthand, essential supplies and June 30 lifting; de facto boundary language preserves territorial qualification.

summary: The Banki–Amchidé commercial crossing between Nigeria and Cameroon was closed in 2014 amid Boko Haram violence and security operations. An official reopening ceremony took place on 15 May 2019, restoring formal permission for cross-border commerce. Earlier reports of returning traffic concerned other routes or preparations rather than a confirmed reopening of this crossing. The original starting day and any exceptional movements during the restriction remain uncertain.

verification.notes: Verified 2014 year-level onset and May 15 official commerce ceremony, excluding earlier reports about other crossings or unfinished preparations.

summary: Mauritania and Mali jointly restricted passenger movement across their border from 24 March 2020 to reduce COVID-19 transmission, while exempting goods trucks. Earlier Mauritanian routing controls had left some Mali-facing posts open and were a separate measure. Special entry authorisations later existed, and by June 2022 ordinary documents were again accepted for Malian and Mauritanian nationals. That later change does not establish an uninterrupted passenger closure or an exact first reopening for everyone.

verification.notes: Confirmed the March 24 bilateral passenger measure and goods exemption, distinct from March 15 routing, with June 2022 access limited to the named nationalities.

summary: Guinea ordered a thirty-day restriction on land-border passenger entry and exit from 27 March 2020 as part of its COVID-19 response. Freight remained permitted with limited crews and monitoring. Transport representatives were still protesting the passenger prohibition in July, when aviation restrictions were eased separately. Later political and coup-related border closures followed different decisions and do not establish when this original health restriction ended.

verification.notes: Checked the March 27 thirty-day order, restricted cargo crews and July continuing passenger prohibition; later political closures do not supply the health-rule endpoint.

summary: Boko Haram violence disrupted ordinary trade at Fotokol–Gambaru between Cameroon and Nigeria for a prolonged period before a limited reopening in late 2016. By December, people and goods were reported crossing the El Beid bridge on specified days after inspection, using porters, bicycles and carts rather than loaded trucks. Accounts differ over the original closure’s timing. The small reopening restored some commerce but did not establish unrestricted freight access or a continuous total closure until later years.

verification.notes: Verified limited people/goods passage by December 2016, specified operating days and inspected small-scale transport; conflicting earlier onset accounts remain unresolved.

summary: Sudanese authorities were reported stopping people and goods at Gallabat–Metema on 21–22 May 2022 after local killings, kidnappings and public demands for security. A civilian truck obstruction had occurred beforehand as a separate action. One report described a reopening agreement on 21 May, while another still found the crossing closed the following day. The conflicting accounts leave the first actual reopening uncertain, and the later June closure cannot be treated as continuous with this episode.

verification.notes: Compared the state-closure account with separate civilian obstruction and conflicting May 21 agreement/May 22 restriction; June–July events are not merged.

summary: Armed forces repeatedly obstructed Tigrayan civilians trying to flee Ethiopia towards Sudan during the Tigray conflict in 2020–2021. Reports describe selective refusals on western routes towards Hamdayet and an interception near Humera on 19 April 2021, while other people succeeded in escaping. These were repeated barriers to a particular civilian group’s exit rather than a documented sealing of the entire frontier. The sources do not establish one uninterrupted closure or a common stated motive for every incident.

verification.notes: Verified December blocking, March retrospective obstruction and April 19 Humera interception, with successful flight excluding a complete frontier seal or continuous spell.

summary: Protesters blocked the Gallabat–Metema road crossing and market on 30–31 January 2021 after traders were abducted, reportedly by Ethiopian militia. The sit-in was still reported on 1 February and disrupted cross-border traffic and trade. Sources disagree over the number abducted and do not establish the exact extent of movement stopped. Later access after a separate closure does not reveal when this protest ended or show that its blockade continued into 2022.

verification.notes: Checked January 30–31 onset alternatives and February 1 continued protest, preserving disputed abduction counts and not using March 2022 access as this protest’s endpoint.

summary: A dispute over the handover of people transported from Guinea to Sierra Leone temporarily interrupted the Gbalamuya crossing on 11 December 2024. Sierra Leonean authorities questioned the deportees’ nationality and refused admission during the standoff, while the two sides gave differing accounts of the notification process. Normal operations had resumed by 13 December. Reports describe an hours-long impasse but do not establish that all traffic was stopped continuously until that later confirmation.

verification.notes: Confirmed December 11 standoff after earlier transport, disputed nationality/notification and normal service by December 13; hours-long reporting is not stretched into a two-day closure.

summary: Togolese authorities temporarily closed part of the Ghana frontier near Mango during unrest in 2017. Reports described refugees, including women, using unofficial paths into Ghana while normal frontier access was restricted. A contemporary account placed reopening by 12 November. The precise post, original closure date and official reason were not established, so the episode cannot be extended to all Togo–Ghana crossings or assigned a reliable duration.

verification.notes: Checked the original report metadata supporting November 12 return, northern-frontier geography and unofficial refugee movement; no Aflao or national closure is inferred.

summary: The international ferry at Rosso between Senegal and Mauritania stopped for about five hours on 5 April 2021 during an authorised protest by pirogue operators. Senegal requested the temporary suspension until the protest ended, and ferry services resumed that evening. The operators were protesting their prolonged loss of activity, but their wider small-boat dispute was separate from this short ferry interruption. A later protest on 8 April did not extend the same stoppage.

verification.notes: Verified April 5 five-hour ferry stoppage at Senegal’s request and evening resumption, distinct from prolonged pirogue restrictions and the April 8 protest.

summary: Senegalese freight vehicles were required to unload cargo for transfer to local trucks when entering Mauritania, with the arrangement documented by March 2018 at Rosso. Participant accounts also describe reciprocal limits on Mauritanian vehicles, while the goods themselves continued moving. A new bilateral transport agreement took effect in July 2025, and later official reporting described restrictions lifted from November. Those policy accounts do not establish the first restored through-truck journey, original onset or uniform enforcement throughout.

verification.notes: Compared WTO’s documented transfer requirement with participant claims of reciprocal limits, July formal abolition and November later reporting; no first through-truck journey is asserted.

summary: An October 2013 customs notice reaffirmed Côte d’Ivoire’s longstanding prohibition on exporting coffee, cocoa and cashew by land, directing exports through designated maritime offices at Abidjan and San-Pedro. The rule targeted these commodities rather than ordinary travellers or unrelated goods. Officials linked cocoa enforcement to economic protection, and customs reported seizing Burkina-bound coffee inland in April 2026. Such enforcement confirms the restriction’s continued use without demonstrating that every illicit shipment was stopped.

verification.notes: Checked the 2013 notice recalling the older commodity-specific rule, designated maritime offices, economic-protection attribution and April 2026 inland coffee seizure.

summary: Grande Barrière between Goma and Gisenyi was closed to passenger movement during the morning of 5 November 2024 for a ministerial security ceremony. Travellers were diverted to Petite Barrière, so the interruption did not close both city crossings. The exact stopping and reopening hours were not reported. A later visit found both posts operating normally, confirming eventual access without showing that the November interruption lasted until that visit.

verification.notes: Verified the November 5 morning passenger interruption and diversion to Petite Barrière, with January normal operation serving only as later access evidence.

summary: Sudanese authorities suspended passengers travelling from Gallabat towards Ethiopia on 19–20 November 2023 after attacks and robberies targeting travellers, while trade continued. Later reporting described Sudanese arrivals receiving transit visas at Metema, and refugee monitoring documented families entering in early January 2024. Those observations establish subsequent access in the same direction, but do not identify the first reopening or show that every traveller regained eligibility together.

verification.notes: Added 2024 to the January admission observation to make the year transition explicit; retained passenger-only direction and continuing trade.

summary: Sudanese police suspended passenger travel processing from Gallabat towards Ethiopia by 3 August 2023, citing safety concerns during fighting in Amhara. An 8 August order allowed foreign nationals to leave Sudan and stranded Sudanese to return, but thousands were still reported waiting at Metema. Officials described some arrivals and departures on 12 August, while UNHCR dated a partial reopening to 13 August. These limited resumptions do not establish a single reopening for all travellers.

verification.notes: Compared August 3 processing suspension, August 8 categorical permission and separate August 12/13 partial movements; no universal first reopening is inferred.

summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo introduced restrictions on international departures on 24 June 2026 to control Ebola transmission. Contacts, response personnel and people who had stayed in affected provinces faced different twenty-one-day requirements, with permission exceptions for some groups. A July amendment replaced systematic quarantine with individual risk assessment, allowing lower-risk groups to travel under monitoring while retaining restrictions for the highest-risk group. This was a targeted health rule, not a blanket ban on all passengers.

verification.notes: Checked June decree articles and permission exceptions against July reporting of superseding risk categories; October summaries of old rules do not extend them unchanged.

summary: Eritrea was reported to have suspended the admission of Sudanese passengers at Laffa by 20 November 2023 because hotels and other facilities were overcrowded. The report did not give the original starting date or establish whether freight and other nationalities were affected. Subsequent discussions concerned preparations for future reopening and passenger coordination, rather than confirmed admission. The first restored access for the affected Sudanese travellers remains unknown.

verification.notes: Verified Laffa’s separate Sudanese-admission suspension and overcrowding attribution, without borrowing Gallabat’s Sunday onset or mistaking December preparations for actual opening.

summary: Djibouti suspended formal reception and registration of asylum seekers arriving from Somalia at Loyada after the May 2014 al-Shabaab attack, according to UNHCR. The agency was still calling for asylum access to reopen in October 2017, while noting that some people entered informally. This restriction concerned formal asylum admission rather than all passengers or goods. Later refugee totals and migrant-centre reports do not establish when that specific access was restored.

verification.notes: Confirmed UNHCR’s May 2014 suspension and October 2017 asylum-specific continuation, with informal entry and unrelated migrant-centre information kept separate.

summary: Non-exempt passenger movement at Moyale between Kenya and Ethiopia was restricted in late March 2020 during the COVID-19 response. Goods vehicles could still cross with a driver and one assistant, subject to health screening, while trenches and patrols sought to prevent unauthorised passenger entry. Passenger restrictions were still reported in June. Later official visitor statistics demonstrate restored Kenya-bound access, but do not identify the first reopening or show that a new border facility itself ended the restriction.

verification.notes: Checked March Moyale passenger restrictions, screened limited cargo crews, June no-passenger report and later Kenya-inbound visitor count without using facility inauguration as reopening.

summary: Truck drivers blocked Kenya’s Malaba exit towards Uganda in May 2020, protesting what they described as harassment and COVID-19 rules; officials disputed that account. Uganda-bound freight was obstructed, while pedestrians and motorcycles could pass nearby approaches. Truck movement resumed on 26 May, but clearing the backlog took longer. Reports differ over the blockade’s exact beginning and interruptions, so queues after reopening cannot be counted as continued closure.

verification.notes: Compared conflicting May blockade beginnings with May 26 resumed trucks, pedestrian/motorcycle access and the separate backlog-clearance period; motives remain attributed.

summary: Traders and clearing agents disrupted freight movements and customs paperwork at Busia on 23 March 2021 in protest against Kenyan maize controls and police fines. Trucks in both directions were delayed for several hours, but a general passenger stoppage was not established. Later reports showed maize trucks and clearance work operating again. They do not identify the precise end of this protest, whose duration must be kept separate from the longer commodity restrictions.

verification.notes: Verified the March 23 freight/paperwork protest and several-hour report, then later Kenya-bound maize clearance without assigning the protest an unsupported endpoint.

summary: Kenyan controls held maize consignments arriving from Uganda at Busia and from Tanzania at Namanga in March–April 2021, with authorities citing contamination concerns. Some stocks were returned, while officials disputed descriptions of a blanket import ban. A 7 May instruction lifted restrictions subject to certification and safety conditions, and maize passage was observed at Busia on 10 May and subsequently reported at Namanga. The evidence concerns maize consignments, not a general closure to other goods or passengers.

verification.notes: Checked commodity-specific holds at both posts, contamination attribution and blanket-ban denial, followed by May 7 conditional lifting and separate observed returns.

summary: Customs and control offices at Karombo and Goli–Anzida on the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Uganda frontier were reported closed on 14 May 2020 following a civil-society appeal for peace and local safety. The interruption affected official processing, while other security services continued operating. Later reports document customs activity again, but do not establish the first reopening after this protest. Closure of service offices does not by itself prove that every passenger or informal movement stopped.

verification.notes: Confirmed DGDA/OCC office closures at the named posts and continuing intelligence services; later customs activity does not establish first reopening or all-passenger denial.

summary: Uganda imposed restrictions on non-exempt movement to and from the Democratic Republic of the Congo on 27 May 2026 during the Ebola response. Response workers, humanitarian operations, food and cargo movements, and security personnel had authorised exceptions, with later limited permissions for medical referrals. Reports at Kasindi–Mpondwe described continuing disruption alongside authorised and irregular crossings. Subsequent changes in enforcement do not establish a continuously sealed frontier or a single reopening for all traveller groups.
